nameStory: The Northern Shortfin Squid gets its name from its relatively short fins compared to other squid species, and its northern range extending from Florida all the way to Greenland and Iceland. The 'shortfin' part refers to the triangular fins that don't extend along the full length of its body like some of its cousins.
description: The Northern Shortfin Squid is a fast-swimming marine mollusk with ten arms, including two longer tentacles, and a torpedo-shaped body built for speed. Like all squids, it has large eyes, can change color rapidly, and moves by jet propulsion, shooting water from its body cavity. These are relatively small squids, typically fitting comfortably in your hand when fully grown. They're incredibly short-lived animals, with most individuals living less than a year in their cold Atlantic waters.

idTips.label: Body shape and fins
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped body with distinctive triangular fins that are noticeably shorter than the body length, giving it a compact, muscular appearance compared to longer-finned squid species

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Ten arms total - eight shorter arms arranged in a circle around the mouth, plus two longer tentacles with paddle-like clubs at the tips for catching prey

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Smooth, rubbery skin that can rapidly shift from translucent white to mottled reddish-brown; when fresh, the skin feels firm and slightly slippery to the touch

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Proportionally large, dark eyes that appear almost black and glassy, positioned on either side of the head and roughly the size of a marble on adult specimens

idTips.label: Internal shell
idTips.description: Contains a clear, plastic-like internal shell called a pen that you can feel as a firm ridge running down the back of the body when gently pressed

habitat: Northern Shortfin Squids live in the open waters of the North Atlantic, from the surface down to deeper waters over the continental shelf. In New England waters, they're most commonly found offshore in the cooler waters of the Gulf of Maine and along the continental shelf edge. You're most likely to encounter them when they're caught by fishermen or occasionally washed up on beaches during storms.

seasonality.spring: Squid begin moving into New England waters as temperatures warm, though they remain primarily offshore in deeper waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Northern Shortfin Squid in New England waters, when they're most active and commonly caught by commercial and recreational fishermen.
seasonality.fall: Still abundant in New England waters through early fall, but begin their southward migration as water temperatures start to drop.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from New England's near-shore waters, having migrated south to warmer Atlantic waters off the mid-Atlantic states.

funFact: These squids are incredible speed demons of the sea - they can actually launch themselves completely out of the water and glide through the air for short distances, earning their family the nickname 'flying squids,' and they achieve this by shooting water so forcefully from their bodies that they become living jet planes.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with longfin squid, but Northern Shortfin Squid has distinctly shorter, more triangular fins that don't run the full length of the body. Remember: 'shortfin' means the fins look stubby compared to the torpedo body, while longfin squid have fins that extend much further along their sides.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'squid,' these animals are actually more closely related to octopuses than to fish, belonging to the group called cephalopods (meaning 'head-foot') because their arms and tentacles emerge directly from their heads. The commercial squid you find in restaurants is often this very species, making it one of the most economically important cephalopods in North American waters.
compareHints: The Northern Shortfin Squid is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to other squid species in New England like the longfin squid, it's distinguished by its shorter fins, more compact body shape, and typically smaller size. Unlike bottom-dwelling squid species, Northern Shortfin Squid are active swimmers that spend their time in open water rather than near the seafloor.
